title: The Most Important Thing I Built This Year
author: thepatrickdempsey
summary: Patrick Dempsey describes building a comprehensive AI-assisted curriculum design system over the past year -- not an AI tool for students, but a backend process that allows him to design richer, more differentiated, more coherent lessons in a fraction of the time. The piece opens with the 'Grammarly objection': critics who say AI-assisted lesson planning is like using Grammarly for essays -- it helps you do the task but doesn't make you a better educator. Dempsey rejects this framing and argues that the opposite is true: the system he built has made him a more thoughtful curriculum designer, not less, because it offloads the production work and frees cognitive bandwidth for the thinking work. The piece's deeper argument is about what schools are actually teaching beyond tool proficiency: they teach the capacity to hold a complex problem in mind, to notice what's missing, to design coherently across a week or a unit. AI can assist those capacities but cannot replace them, and the designer who uses AI well has developed more of those capacities, not fewer.
points: * Dempsey's AI-assisted curriculum design system offloads production work (formatting, differentiation scaffolds, resource compilation) to free cognitive bandwidth for the design thinking work that actually produces educational quality. * The 'Grammarly objection' misidentifies where the skill in curriculum design lives: it is not in the production of materials but in the thinking about learning sequences, gaps, and coherence -- capacities that AI assistance can develop, not replace. * The system Dempsey built has made him a more thoughtful curriculum designer because faster production cycles mean more iterations, more revision, and more time to think about the learning theory behind the choices. * Schools teach capacities beyond tool proficiency: holding a complex problem in mind, noticing what's missing, designing coherently across time -- these are the capacities that AI cannot replace and that good AI use develops. * The distinction between AI as production assistant and AI as thinking partner is the key variable: production assistance frees the designer's mind for thinking; thinking partnership develops the designer's mind through challenge and dialogue.
quotes: The Grammarly objection to AI in lesson planning goes like this: you're outsourcing the cognitive work, so you're not developing as an educator. You're just getting the output faster. This objection assumes that the cognitive work in curriculum design is in the production of the materials. It's not. It's in the thinking about learning.

I've designed more units this year than in any previous year. I've also revised more, thrown more away, and started over more. The speed of production is not making me lazier. It's making iteration cheap enough to be habitual. That is making me a better designer.

What I built this year is not an AI lesson planner. It's a curriculum design environment where AI handles the parts I shouldn't be spending my mental energy on so that I can spend my mental energy on the parts that actually matter.

Schools are not teaching tool proficiency. They're teaching the capacity to hold a hard problem in your mind for a week without losing the thread. To notice what's missing from an argument. To design a sequence of experiences that builds toward something real. AI doesn't do any of that. But the designer who has used AI well has done more of it, not less.

The difference between AI as production assistant and AI as thinking partner is the most important distinction in this whole conversation. Production assistance makes you faster. Thinking partnership makes you better. They are different relationships, and building the right one is the work.
